theory.intro: The derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$, and the derivative of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$. These formulas hold only when $x$ is measured in **radians**. Sums and constant multiples differentiate term by term.
facts: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x$, so differentiating cosine introduces a negative sign.
Both formulas require $x$ in **radians**; they are false when $x$ is measured in degrees.
A constant multiple stays out the front: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(k\sin x) = k\cos x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(k\cos x) = -k\sin x$.
When $x$ is multiplied inside, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin kx) = k\cos kx$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos kx) = -k\sin kx$.
Differentiate a sum one term at a time, using the power rule on any $x^{n}$ terms.
Differentiating repeatedly cycles $\sin x \to \cos x \to -\sin x \to -\cos x \to \sin x$, returning to the start after four steps.
steps: Differentiate each term separately, keeping any constant multiple out the front.
Multiply by the coefficient of $x$ inside the function.

workedExamples.question_text: Differentiate (a) $y=8\sin x$ and (b) $y=-6\cos x$. Angles are measured in radians.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Keep the constant multiple.
$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=8\cos x\end{align*}$
(b) Differentiating cosine introduces a negative sign.
$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=-6(-\sin x)\\&=6\sin x\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Differentiate (a) $y=4\sin 6x$ and (b) $y=10\cos\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)$. Angles are measured in radians.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply by the coefficient of $x$ inside each function.
(a)
$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=4\times6\cos 6x\\&=24\cos 6x\end{align*}$
(b)
$\begin{align*}\frac{dy}{dx}&=10\left(-\frac14\sin\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)\right)\\&=-\frac52\sin\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Differentiate $y=3x^4+2\sin(2\pi x)-4\cos(3x)$. Angles are measured in radians.
Given $f(x)=4\cos 3x$, find $f'(x)$ and the exact value of $f'\left(\frac{\pi}{18}\right)$. Angles are measured in radians.
Find the first, second, third and fourth derivatives of $y=12\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$. Angles are measured in radians.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply by $\frac12$ at each differentiation, retaining the constant already obtained.
$\begin{align*}y'&=12\times\frac12\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\\&=6\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}y''&=6\left(-\frac12\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right)\\&=-3\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}y'''&=-3\times\frac12\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\\&=-\frac32\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}y''''&=-\frac32\left(-\frac12\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right)\\&=\frac34\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=3\sin 2x$ where $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, in exact general form and in the form $y=mx+b$. Angles are measured in radians.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=6\cos 2x$.
At $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, the tangent gradient is
$\begin{align*}m&=6\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=3\end{align*}$
The point has ordinate
$\begin{align*}y&=3\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$
Use the point and gradient.
$\begin{align*}y-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}&=3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\y&=3x+\frac{3\sqrt3-\pi}{2}\end{align*}$
In exact general form,
$6x-2y+3\sqrt3-\pi=0$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the equation of the normal to $y=2\cos x$ where $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, in exact general form. Angles are measured in radians.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\frac{dy}{dx}=-2\sin x$.
At $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$, the tangent gradient is
$\begin{align*}m_{\mathrm{tangent}}&=-2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\&=-1\end{align*}$
The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal:
$m_{\mathrm{normal}}=-\frac{1}{-1}=1$.
The point has ordinate
$\begin{align*}y&=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\\&=\sqrt3\end{align*}$
Use the point and normal gradient.
$\begin{align*}y-\sqrt3&=x-\frac{\pi}{6}\\6y-6\sqrt3&=6x-\pi\end{align*}$
In exact general form,
$6x-6y+6\sqrt3-\pi=0$.

mastery.question_text: Find the equation of the tangent to $y = \sin 2x$ at the point where $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, in exact general form.
Find the equation of the normal to $y = 4\cos x$ at the point where $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, in exact general form.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -4\sin x$
At $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$= -4 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$= -2\sqrt{3}$
The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal:
$m = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$
$= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$
$y = 4\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$= 2$
$y - 2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$
$18y - 36 = 3\sqrt{3}x - \sqrt{3}\pi$
$3\sqrt{3}x - 18y - \sqrt{3}\pi + 36 = 0$
